facts.fact_text: On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
The applicants in the Chrysostomos and Papachrysostomou v. Turkey cases also took part in the anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia on 19 July 1989.
The applicant in the Loizidou v. Turkey case also took part in the anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia on 19 July 1989.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant at Nicosia District Court on 10 April 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant at Nicosia District Court on 10 April 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held on the fifteenth anniversary of the Turkish intervention in Cyprus.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant at Nicosia District Court on 10 April 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was held in support of the missing persons and to protest against human-rights violations.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant at Nicosia District Court on 10 April 2000, the applicant and other women had planned to gather in the grounds of the Ayios Kassianos School and to stage a sit-in in protest against the occupation of the northern part of Cyprus.

According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant at Nicosia District Court on 10 April 2000, the applicant and other women asked the Bishop of Kitium to conduct a service in the St. George's Chapel, which was located near the Ayios Kassianos School.
When the applicant arrived at the Ayios Kassianos School grounds, the grounds were filled with a group of mostly young women who were singing.
The applicant noticed the presence of Turkish policemen armed with batons at the Ayios Kassianos School grounds.
The UN officers invited the demonstrators at the Ayios Kassianos School grounds to leave the premises.
Within a matter of seconds of the UN officers' invitation to leave, Turkish policemen rushed towards the demonstrators at the Ayios Kassianos School grounds.
Some of the women demonstrators at the Ayios Kassianos School grounds were grabbed by their clothes and hit with guns and batons by Turkish policemen.
The applicant was hit and pushed by Turkish policemen at the Ayios Kassianos School grounds.
The applicant received what she described as a 'terrible blow in the right leg beneath the tibia'.
The applicant stated that she had been hit with a sharp object, namely a bayonet wielded by a Turkish soldier.
The applicant's leg started to bleed profusely after she was struck.
The applicant felt herself drifting into unconsciousness after being struck.
The applicant shouted: 'Help, help, please, I am losing my leg'.
Some demonstrators put the applicant on a stretcher after she was struck.
The applicant was taken by ambulance to Nicosia General Hospital after being struck at the Ayios Kassianos School grounds.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment.

The Government alleged that the demonstrators were warned in Greek and English that unless they dispersed they would be arrested in accordance with the laws of the 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' ('TRNC').
The Government alleged that the applicant was arrested by the Turkish-Cypriot police after crossing the UN buffer zone and entering the area under Turkish-Cypriot control.

The Government alleged that the Turkish-Cypriot police intervened in the face of the manifest inability of the Greek-Cypriot authorities and the UN Force in Cyprus to contain the incursion and its possible consequences.
The Government alleged that no force was used against demonstrators who did not intrude into the 'TRNC' border area.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.
The Government alleged that no one was ill-treated during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The Government alleged that it was possible that some of the demonstrators had hurt themselves in the confusion or in attempting to scale barbed wire or other fencing.

The Government alleged that had the Turkish police, or anyone else, assaulted or beaten any of the demonstrators, the UN Secretary General would no doubt have referred to this in his report to the Security Council.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code defines an unlawful assembly as occurring where five or more persons assemble with intent to commit an offence, or, being assembled with intent to carry out some common purpose, conduct themselves in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear that the persons so assembled will commit a breach of the peace or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to commit a breach of the peace.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that it is immaterial that the original assembly was lawful if, being assembled, the persons conduct themselves with a common purpose in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear a breach of the peace.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that when an unlawful assembly has begun to execute its purpose by a breach of the peace and to the terror of the public, the assembly is called a riot and the persons assembled are said to be riotously assembled.
According to section 71 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, any person who takes part in an unlawful assembly is guilty of a misdemeanour and liable to imprisonment for one year.

Section 80 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that any person who carries in public without lawful occasion any offensive arm or weapon in such a manner as to cause terror to any person is guilty of a misdemeanour and is liable to imprisonment for two years, and his arms or weapons shall be forfeited.
According to section 82 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, it is an offence to carry a knife outside the home.

Chapter 155, section 14(1)(b) of the Cypriot Criminal Procedure Law states that any police officer may, without warrant, arrest any person who commits in his presence any offence punishable with imprisonment.

Chapter 155, section 14(1)(c) of the Cypriot Criminal Procedure Law states that any police officer may, without warrant, arrest any person who obstructs a police officer while in the execution of his duty.

Section 9 of Law No. 5/72 states that any person who enters a prohibited military area without authorization, or by stealth, or fraudulently, shall be tried by a military court in accordance with the Military Offences Act, and those found guilty shall be punished.
Subsection 12(1) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that no person shall enter or leave the Colony except through an approved port.

Subsection 12(5) of the Aliens and Immigration Law states that any person who contravenes or fails to observe any of the provisions of subsections (1), (2), (3) or (4) of section 12 shall be guilty of an offence and shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months or to a fine not exceeding one hundred pounds or to both such imprisonment and fine.
The Government alleged that the applicant had participated in a violent demonstration with the aim of inflaming anti-Turkish sentiment.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were supported by the Greek-Cypriot administration and were demanding that the 'Green Line' in Nicosia should be dismantled.
The Government alleged that some demonstrators carried Greek flags, clubs, knives and wire-cutters.
The Government alleged that the demonstrators were acting in a provocative manner and shouting abuse.

The Government alleged that in the case of demonstrators who were arrested for violating the border, no more force was used than was reasonably necessary in the circumstances in order to arrest and detain the persons concerned.
The Government alleged that no one was ill-treated during the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
The Government alleged that it was possible that some of the demonstrators had hurt themselves in the confusion or in attempting to scale barbed wire or other fencing.

The Government alleged that had the Turkish police, or anyone else, assaulted or beaten any of the demonstrators, the UN Secretary General would no doubt have referred to this in his report to the Security Council.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by the UN Force in Cyprus (UNFICYP) and destroyed a UNFICYP observation post.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that Turkish-Cypriot police and security forces elements forced their way into the Ayios Kassianos area and apprehended 111 persons, 101 of them women.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that the Ayios Kassianos school complex is situated in the UN buffer zone, but that the Turkish forces claim it to be on their side of the cease-fire line.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that under working arrangements with UNFICYP, the Turkish-Cypriot security forces had patrolled the Ayios Kassianos school grounds for several years within specific restrictions, and that this patrolling had ceased altogether as part of an unmanning agreement implemented in May 1989.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that in the afternoon of 21 July 1989, some 300 Greek Cypriots gathered at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia to protest the continuing detention by the Turkish-Cypriot authorities of those apprehended at Ayios Kassianos.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that the number of demonstrators at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia fluctuated between 200 and 2,000 and that they blocked all UN traffic through that entrance until 30 July 1989, when the Turkish-Cypriot authorities released the last two detainees.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that the events of 19 July 1989 created considerable tension in Cyprus and that intensive efforts were made, both at UN headquarters and at Nicosia, to contain and resolve the situation.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that on 21 July 1989, the UN Secretary General expressed his concern at the events that had taken place and stressed that it was vital that all parties keep in mind the purpose of the UN buffer zone as well as their responsibility to ensure that that area was not violated.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that on 21 July 1989, the UN Secretary General urged the Turkish-Cypriot authorities to release without delay all those who had been detained.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that on 24 July 1989, the President of the Security Council announced that he had conveyed to the representatives of all the parties, on behalf of the members of the Council, the Council's deep concern at the tense situation created by the incidents of 19 July 1989.

The UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989 stated that the President of the Security Council stressed the need strictly to respect the UN buffer zone and appealed for the immediate release of all persons still detained, and asked all concerned to show maximum restraint and to take urgent steps to bring about a relaxation of tension.

Three witnesses who saw the wound being inflicted on the applicant on 19 July 1989 — two friends and the editor of a local newspaper — had already died by the time of the proceedings.
An affidavit sworn by a witness, Mrs Olga Nicolaidou, corroborated the applicant's version of events regarding the demonstration of 19 July 1989.
In support of her claim of ill-treatment, the applicant produced a medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou, a specialist orthopaedic surgeon practising in Nicosia.

The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou stated that the applicant was injured on 19 July 1989 by Turks following an attack on women near Ayios Kassianos in Nicosia at the Ayios Kassianos Primary School.

The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou recorded that the applicant sustained an injury to the right lower limb of the upper third of the tibia with an open wound about 9 centimetres long.
The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou stated that the applicant's wound was caused with a sharp object.
The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou recorded that treatment of the applicant included surgical cleaning of the wound.
The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou recorded that treatment of the applicant included stitching up of the wound.
The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou recorded that treatment of the applicant included pharmaceutical treatment.
The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou recorded that treatment of the applicant included regular dressing of the wound.
The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou recorded that treatment of the applicant included complete rest in bed for ten days with the leg supported by pillows.
The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou recorded that the stitches were removed ten days after the applicant's treatment.
The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou recorded that the applicant was required to walk with crutches for one month.

The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou recorded that the applicant's present condition included an evident ugly scar of about 9 centimetres in the upper third of the tibia, transversal.
The medical certificate issued on 27 March 2000 by Doctor Stelios Georgiou recorded that the applicant's present condition included loss of feeling in the area of the wound.
